title: Sacred buildings
hook: cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: visit as a respectful guest

segments.voice: Yesterday, a newborn, and your line was new: a face seen as if for the first time. Whose face did you look at? Today we end the week inside a building made for awe. Day one thousand forty-three.

A heavy door swings shut behind you, and the street noise is gone. The ceiling is higher than it needs to be. The light comes in at an angle. Somewhere, someone is praying quietly, and you lower your voice without being asked. Cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: people have built rooms like this on purpose, rooms that change how you stand and how loud you speak. You don't have to share the faith of a place to honor its hush. You only have to come in the way a guest comes into someone's home.
screen: `THE DOOR SWINGS SHUT.` → `A CEILING HIGHER THAN IT NEEDS TO BE.` → `COME IN AS A GUEST.`

segments.voice: First, a place that turned out to be holy. In Genesis, Jacob is on the run, sleeping in the open with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." There's no building yet. Just a man waking up to where he is. Second, watching your step. Ecclesiastes has advice for anyone walking into a house of worship. In the King James words: "Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear." Mind your feet; listen more than you speak. Holy places often ask something of the body first: shoes off in some, heads covered in others, voices lowered. The body learns respect before the mind has words for it. Third, being a guest. A sacred building is someone's spiritual home. A guest doesn't need to believe what the hosts believe, or pretend to. A guest dresses with care, asks at the door what's expected, watches what others do, and doesn't take photos of people at prayer without asking. Some places of worship welcome visitors at set hours, or have a person who will show you around. Fourth, what a guest receives. You may not pray there. You may not understand everything you see. But you'll stand where other people have brought their joys and griefs, and some visitors say they can feel that weight in the room. Jacob's words fit many first visits: a place that meant more than it looked, and I knew it not.
screen: `JACOB: AND I KNEW IT NOT.` · `ECCLESIASTES: KEEP THY FOOT.` · `A GUEST IN SOMEONE'S HOME.` · `WHAT A GUEST RECEIVES.` · then, large: `THE GATE OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: If there's a place of worship near you, plan a visit this week as a guest. For now, begin with photos. Find a picture of the inside of one sacred building, a cathedral, a mosque, a temple, a gurdwara, a synagogue. Look at it slowly. Which way are people meant to face? Where does the eye go first? Where would you stand if you walked in? Imagine lowering your voice at the door. If you pray, you can let this be a quiet greeting to the place. If you don't, simply stand there as a guest. The bell holds the time.
Sacred buildings. Rooms made on purpose to change how you stand and speak, visited not as a tourist, but as a guest. Today's word.

Your line: as a guest. This week we went looking for awe on purpose: one tree, small things up close, water, the storm, the music, a newborn, and now a sacred room. Pick one to keep. Today, walk past a place of worship and notice its door. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: Churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras and synagogues often welcome respectful visitors; guests typically dress modestly, follow the house customs on shoes and head coverings, and ask before taking photos.

fork.setup: you're Jacob. you wake from a dream of a ladder reaching to heaven, in an empty place with a stone for a pillow. what do you say?
options: "surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not."
fork.reveal: Genesis 28: Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place, "and I knew it not", and calls it the gate of heaven, with no building in sight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sacred building is only for its members.
what it means: a guest can visit with respect, and the room itself can teach awe.
what a scholar hears: in Genesis 28, Jacob names a bare place "the house of God" before any building stands there.
